To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the variance of the difference between two proportions is equal to the sum of their variances, and 2) the variance of a difference between two proportions, when one is estimated from a stratified sample, is approximately equal to the sum, over strata, of the product of the sample size in the stratum and the square of the difference between the strata’s proportions.
the use of the ratio estimator in the presence of a stratified random sample leads to a bias in the estimate of variance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of estimating the variance of a ratio estimator in the case of a stratified sample.
the development of an algorithm to estimate a variance of the ratio estimator.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in stratified samples, there are three possible sources of error in computing variance of ratio estimates, namely, (1) sampling errors, (2) errors in estimating the variances of the variables used for stratification, and (3) errors in estimating variances of the ratio estimates.

the use of a ratio estimator is a good idea, provided the sample size is sufficiently large and the variance of the ratio estimator is not too large compared with the variance of the direct estimator.
there is no evidence that the use of the ratio estimator in the analysis of the data from the 1950 census was responsible for the observed bias in the estimates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that it is possible to obtain an estimate of the population mean that is more accurate than the sample mean.

, in stratified samples, a gross error in the numerator variable will not be detected by the usual rel-variance check unless the error is also present in the variable used for strata, and that a gross error in either the numerator or strata variable will not be found by the rel-variance check if the other variable is also grossly in error.
the variance of the stratified sample mean of the variable used in stratification is not negligible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the variance of a ratio estimate can be much larger than the corresponding rel-variances of the numerator and denominator variables.
the variance of the stratum totals is often a good estimate of the variance of the stratified sample.

, for a given rel-variance, the upper bounds of the variance of the ratio estimate are smaller for stratification by the numerator of the ratio than for stratification by either of the variables in the denominator.
